newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Manila aims to have scripless system by late '96.
newsitem.headline: Manila aims to have scripless system by late '96.

text.p: Delayed by six months, the Philippines should have a long-awaited scripless equities trading system up and running by year-end.
"I hope it's operational by Christmas, if not sooner," Roman Azanza, chairman of the Philippines' Capital Markets Development Council (CMDC), said in an interview.

The CMDC advises President Fidel Ramos on capital market reforms. It comprises the heads of the Central Bank, Finance Ministry, Philippine Stock Exchange, Securities and Exchange Commission, and private groups such as the Bankers Association, the Investment Houses Association, and the Financial Executives Institute.
Outgoing Philippine Stock Exchange President Eduardo de los Angeles is more optimistic and says the new scripless trading system would be implemented by November 11.
The new system, operating through a computerised central depository that would keep tab of share trades, is designed to minimise opportunities for fraud and speed up stock transfers.

Azanza told Reuters that the central clearing and settlement project should have started operations in April but had been delayed by the need to put a legal and regulatory framework in place to address risks such as default by a broker.

"We want a very good one (in place). The first draft of rules was not good enough. We wanted to clearly identify the risk, how that risk will be fixed if that happens, who's responsible and what are the mechanisms that would be in place to immediately address that risk," he said.
The rules could be finished in two weeks and then submitted to the Securities and Exchange Commission, which will issue a permit allowing full operations to start, Azanza said.

"We're trying to hit a target that within a year 75 percent of the market capital on the exchange will be on the computer," Azanza said, adding that in some countries it took three years to get all shares entered into similar systems.
By the first quarter of 1997, treasury bill trading should also be included in the central depositary, he said.

Under the new system for stocks being set up, settlement on both payments and securities will be finished in four days. Under the present manual system, the investor is required to pay his broker in four days but he gets his security 24 days later.
Clearing and settlement of T-bills, however, will take place the same day, since the Central Bank will act as the clearing bank.
"By closing the gap, you are now cutting immensely the risk of the market and the investor," Azanza said.

Two private companies have been set up to undertake the clearing and settlements and to address the market risks. These are the Philippine Central Depository Inc (PCDI) and the Securities Clearing Corp of the Philippines (SCCP).
The PCDI, which has the Philippine Stock Exchange and the Bankers Association of the Philippines as the biggest stockholders, will oversee the process of clearing and settlements.

The SCCP, which has the Philippine Stock Exchange as the major shareholder, will handle the liquidity and brokers' guarantee fund, which are intended to ease the working capital of a broker and address payments in case of a default.
